title: Core Concepts
subtitle: Foundations of AI, ML & CPMAI
examWeightHint: Appears inside every scenario, every phase.
top10: AI ⊃ ML ⊃ DL ; today's AI is narrow and probabilistic .
AI projects are data projects — data-centric beats model-centric.
DIKUW — climb from raw data toward (human-held) wisdom.
Labels→Supervised, none→Unsupervised, rewards→Reinforcement.
~80%+ failure rate , driven by business/data/management causes.
Each failure cause has a CPMAI phase antidote — know the mapping.
CPMAI = CRISP-DM + agile + AI-specific , six phases, iterative .
Think Big, Start Small, Iterate Often — reject big-bang answers.
Responsible AI in every phase — fairness, explainability, privacy, oversight.
Proxy variables smuggle bias — audit features and subgroups.
revision: AI ⊃ ML ⊃ Deep Learning ; all current AI = narrow ; AI is probabilistic .
DIKUW: Data → Information → Knowledge → Understanding → Wisdom; wisdom stays human.
ML types: Supervised (labels) / Unsupervised (none) / Semi-supervised / Reinforcement (rewards) .
Data-centric > model-centric : fix data before chasing algorithms (GIGO).
~80%+ AI projects fail — for business/data/management reasons, not tech.
Failure causes ↔ CPMAI phase shields (no KPI→I, data surprise→II, prep underrated→III, wrong metric→V, decay→VI, big-bang→iterate).
CPMAI = CRISP-DM + AI-specific + agile ; six phases; iterative ; vendor-neutral.
Think Big, Start Small, Iterate Often.
Responsible AI (fairness, explainability, accountability, privacy, safety, human oversight) runs through every phase ; watch proxy variables .

examTips.heading: Memory Tricks
bullets: Nesting dolls: AI (biggest) → ML → DL (smallest).
DIKUW ladder story: numbers → report → pattern → why → best action.
"Fix the data first" — when a scenario shows messy data + algorithm-hopping, the data-centric answer wins.
Failure question reflex: the cause is business/data/management ~always — never "the algorithm was unlucky."

examTips.heading: Keywords
bullets: " AI projects are data projects "
" Narrow AI ", " probabilistic "
" Iterative , built on CRISP-DM "
" Responsible/trustworthy AI ", " bias ", " explainability "

examTips.heading: Traps
bullets: "Buy a better algorithm to fix bad data" → wrong.
"AI will fully replace human wisdom/judgment" → wrong (top of DIKUW stays human).
"Run CPMAI phases once, sequentially, then done" → wrong (iterate).
"Ethics review only before launch" → wrong (every phase).

title: Phase I — Business Understanding
subtitle: Is this AI? Scope, ROI, patterns, ethics
top10: Phase I comes FIRST — every scenario asking "what should the PM do first?" → understand the business problem .
"Do we even need AI?" — rules/RPA beat AI for deterministic, repetitive tasks.
Every valid AI use case maps to one of the 7 Patterns of AI — memorize all seven with examples.
Success = business KPIs and ROI , never accuracy alone.
The Go/No-Go decision is a Phase I output (P-P-K-F: Problem, Pattern, KPI, Feasibility).
Think Big, Start Small, Iterate Often — reject big-bang answers.
CPMAI = CRISP-DM + AI-specific + agile/iterative enhancements.
Phase I repeats in every iteration — it is not one-time.
Ethics, bias, and regulation are assessed in Phase I, not left for the end.
1 cause of AI project failure = poor business understanding ("solution looking for a problem").
revision: Phase I = Business Understanding = the WHY phase = FIRST phase , repeated every iteration .
Built on CRISP-DM , enhanced with AI-specific + agile practices.
Core question: "Do we even need AI?" → If rules/RPA can solve it, don't use AI .
Map every use case to the 7 Patterns of AI : Hyperpersonalization, Autonomous Systems, Predictive Analytics, Conversation, Patterns & Anomalies, Recognition, Goal-Driven Systems.
Define business KPIs + ROI — accuracy alone ≠ success.
Go/No-Go decision happens in Phase I (P-P-K-F checklist).
Mantra: Think Big, Start Small, Iterate Often.
1 reason AI projects fail: poor business understanding / no clear business problem .
Feasibility check: business, data, tech/skills, ethics/regulatory , operational.
Stakeholders aligned early; expectations set that AI is probabilistic , not perfect.
Output of Phase I: problem statement, pattern mapping, business case (KPI+ROI), constraints, go/no-go, first-iteration scope .
Next phase: Phase II — Data Understanding .

" Do we even need AI? "

examTips.heading: Common Exam Traps to Avoid
bullets: Any answer that says " start by collecting data " or " start by selecting an algorithm " in a new-project scenario → WRONG . Business understanding comes first.
Any answer implying AI should be used for simple rule-based tasks → WRONG (use RPA).
Any answer defining success only by accuracy → WRONG (need business KPI).
"Complete all requirements upfront, then build" (waterfall thinking) → WRONG (CPMAI is iterative).

title: Phase II — Data Understanding
subtitle: Sources, quality, bias, feasibility
examWeightHint: Data-centric thinking is the CPMAI worldview.
top10: Phase II = WHAT data — assessment only; cleaning is Phase III.
Data requirements flow from the Phase I business problem .
GIGO — quality beats quantity.
~ 80% of enterprise data is unstructured .
Big Data V's: Volume, Variety, Velocity, Veracity .
Quality dimensions: Accuracy, Completeness, Consistency, Timeliness, Validity, Uniqueness .
Verify privacy/legal rights (GDPR, HIPAA, DPDP) before using data.
Check quantity and representativeness (bias prevention).
Phase II ends with a data go/no-go decision.
Phase II repeats every iteration .
revision: Phase II = WHAT data — after Phase I, before Phase III, every iteration.
Derive data requirements from the business problem (never data-first).
Data types: structured / semi-structured / unstructured (~ 80% unstructured ).
Sources: internal, external, generated .
Big Data V's: Volume, Variety, Velocity, Veracity (+Value) .
Quality dimensions ( A-CC-TVU ): Accuracy, Completeness, Consistency, Timeliness, Validity, Uniqueness.
GIGO — data quality decides model quality.
Perform EDA ; check quantity sufficiency ; check bias/representativeness .
Verify privacy, consent, regulations (GDPR/HIPAA/DPDP).
Ends with data go/no-go .
Assess in II, fix in III.
knowledgeCheck: Why must data requirements come from the business problem instead of available data?
Explain GIGO with a banking example.

examTips.heading: Memory Tricks
bullets: Phase II = WHAT data (I=WHY, III=HOW to prepare).
Quality dimensions: A-CC-TVU .
GIGO — quality first, always.
" Assess in II, Fix in III " — understanding vs preparation.

examTips.heading: Keywords Signaling Right Answers
bullets: "Identify data requirements from the business problem "
" Assess data quality and quantity"
"Verify data rights/privacy "

examTips.heading: Traps

"Use whatever data we already have" without business mapping → wrong.

title: Phase III — Data Preparation
subtitle: Clean, label, split, engineer features
examWeightHint: Most project time is spent here — 60–80%.
top10: Phase III = biggest effort: 60–80% of the project.
Assess in II, fix in III — cleaning belongs here.
Median imputation beats mean when outliers exist.
Keep outliers in fraud/anomaly use cases.
Feature engineering with domain experts drives performance.
Labeling is costly — plan budget, guidelines, quality checks.
Train/Validation/Test — lock the test set.
Data leakage = inflated lab results, production failure.
Augmentation & synthetic data solve scarcity and privacy limits.
Build automated pipelines — CPMAI iterates.
revision: Phase III = HOW to prepare data — cleaning, transformation, features, labels, splits.
Consumes 60–80% of total project effort — the biggest phase.
Cleaning: missing (impute), duplicates, errors, outliers, standardize .
Don't remove outliers in anomaly/fraud use cases.
Transformation: normalize, standardize, encode (one-hot), bin, aggregate .
Feature engineering (domain-driven new inputs) is a top performance driver.
Labeling enables supervised learning — plan cost, guidelines, quality checks.
Augmentation/synthetic data expand scarce datasets.
Split train/validation/test ; test set stays locked → avoid data leakage .
Fix class imbalance (oversample/undersample/weights).
Automate via pipelines (ETL/ELT) ; version and document everything.

examTips.heading: Memory Tricks
bullets: "80/80 rule": ~80% of data is unstructured (Phase II) and up to ~80% of effort is data prep (Phase III).
Leakage = lying to yourself — great lab scores, dead in production.
Fraud/anomaly projects: outliers are gold , don't delete.
"Assess in II, Fix in III."

examTips.heading: Keywords
bullets: " Clean, transform, feature engineering, labeling "
" Most time-consuming phase "
" Train/validation/test split ", " hold-out test set "

examTips.heading: Traps
bullets: "Spend most time on modeling" → wrong; prep dominates.
"Use the test set to improve the model" → leakage , wrong.
"Delete all outliers" in a fraud scenario → wrong.

title: Phase IV — Model Development
subtitle: Train, iterate, avoid leakage
examWeightHint: PM role is governance, not tuning hyperparameters.
top10: Labels → Supervised; No labels → Unsupervised; Rewards → RL.
Classification = category; Regression = number.
Overfitting: train↑ test↓ → regularization/more data/simpler model.
Underfitting: both↓ → more complexity/better features.
Hyperparameters = human-set , tuned on the validation set only.
Baseline first , then iterate — timebox experiments.
Simplest sufficient model wins ; explainability can beat accuracy.
Phase IV ≈ 10–15% of effort — data prep still dominates.
Cross-validation = reliable performance estimates.
Transfer learning = practical shortcut using pre-trained models.
revision: Phase IV = build & train — only ~ 10–15% of effort .
ML types: Supervised (labeled) / Unsupervised (unlabeled) / Reinforcement (rewards) .
Supervised outputs: Classification = category, Regression = number .
Parameters learned; hyperparameters human-set, tuned on validation set .
Overfitting = memorize (train↑ test↓); fix: regularization, simpler model, more data, early stopping, cross-validation.
Underfitting = too simple (both↓); fix: complexity, better features.
k-fold cross-validation → reliable estimates.
Baseline first → simplest sufficient model → timeboxed iteration.
Explainability can outrank accuracy (regulated industries).
Options: build vs buy/API vs pre-trained fine-tune (transfer learning) .
Version code+data+models for reproducibility .
knowledgeCheck: Classify: predicting tomorrow's electricity demand; grouping news articles by theme; teaching a drone to land via rewards.
Explain parameters vs hyperparameters with one example each.
Describe overfitting using a student analogy and list three remedies.

examTips.heading: Memory Tricks
bullets: "Labels = Supervised" — the word to hunt in every scenario.
Class = Category, Regress = Real number (both start matching letters).
Overfit = Over-memorized (great at home, fails in exam hall).
Hyper = Human — hyperparameters are human-set.
RL keyword scan: reward, agent, environment, trial-and-error, goal .

examTips.heading: Keywords
bullets: " Simplest model that meets the need "
" Baseline first, iterate "
" Explainability for regulators"
" Validation set for tuning "

examTips.heading: Traps
bullets: "Choose deep learning because it's advanced" → wrong; match to need.
"Tune hyperparameters on the test set" → leakage, wrong.
"Training accuracy 99% proves success" → overfitting suspicion.
"Spend most project time perfecting models" → wrong effort model.

title: Phase V — Model Evaluation
subtitle: Metrics, business value, go/no-go
examWeightHint: Accuracy is rarely the right single metric.
top10: Evaluation = technical + business + ethical — all gates must pass.
Precision = TP/(TP+FP); Recall = TP/(TP+FN); F1 = harmonic mean.
Accuracy paradox — never trust accuracy on imbalanced data.
Missing is worse → Recall; False alarm is worse → Precision.
Type I = FP; Type II = FN.
Final metrics come from the locked, untouched test set .
Threshold tradeoffs are business decisions.
Fairness/bias audits are mandatory before deployment.
Validate against Phase I KPIs — lab success ≠ business success.
Deploy / Iterate / Stop — stopping a bad model is good governance.
revision: Phase V = "Good enough?" — technical + business + ethical evaluation.
Use the locked test set for final metrics (first touch!).
Confusion matrix: TP/TN/FP/FN ; Type I = FP, Type II = FN.
Precision = TP/(TP+FP) (predicted); Recall = TP/(TP+FN) (reality); F1 balances both.
Accuracy paradox: imbalanced data → accuracy misleads → use P/R/F1/AUC.
FN-costly (cancer/fraud) → Recall. FP-costly (spam) → Precision.
Regression: MAE, RMSE, R² .
Threshold tradeoff is a business decision (₹ cost of FP vs FN).
Fairness/bias audit + explainability are required gates.
Validate against Phase I business KPIs — technical success alone ≠ success.
Outcomes: Deploy / Iterate / Stop (stop is legitimate!).
knowledgeCheck: Why are two evaluation levels (technical + business) both mandatory?
Given TP=45, FP=15, FN=5, TN=935 — compute accuracy, precision, recall, F1.

examTips.heading: Memory Tricks
bullets: Precision = Predicted; Recall = Reality.
"Cancer & Crime → Recall" (never miss). "Spam → Precision" (never block good mail).
Accuracy + imbalanced data mentioned together = paradox trap → answer uses P/R/F1.
Phase V motto: "Technically good AND business good."

examTips.heading: Keywords
bullets: " Untouched/held-out test set "
" Business KPI validation " against Phase I
" Fairness/bias evaluation "
" Deploy / iterate / stop "

examTips.heading: Traps
bullets: Choosing accuracy for imbalanced scenarios → wrong.
"Model passed metrics, deploy without business review" → wrong.
"Adjust the model using test results repeatedly" → test set contamination.
Sunk-cost reasoning ("we invested too much to stop") → wrong; stop is valid .

title: Phase VI — Operationalization
subtitle: Deploy, monitor, drift, MLOps
examWeightHint: The model is not done until it is in production.
top10: Value begins at deployment — Phase VI is continuous, never "done."
Data drift = inputs shift; Concept drift = meaning shifts.
Monitor performance + drift + business KPI + ops + fairness.
Retrain on schedule or on drift triggers — models decay.
Serving fit: real-time (ms), batch (bulk), edge (on-device) .
Roll out safely: shadow → canary → full , rollback ready.
MLOps = DevOps + data & model versioning + drift management.
Model registry + audit trails + explainability = governance.
Human-in-the-loop for high-stakes decisions.
Learnings loop to Phase I — Iterate Often .
revision: Phase VI = deploy + monitor + maintain — value starts (not ends) at go-live.
Serving modes: batch / real-time / edge (+cloud/on-prem/hybrid).
Rollout ladder: shadow → canary → A/B → full , with rollback ready.
Data drift = input distribution changes; concept drift = X→Y meaning changes.
Monitor: performance, drift, business KPI, operational, fairness — with alert thresholds.
Retraining: scheduled / trigger-based / continuous → mini-cycle through Phases III–V.
MLOps: versioning (code+data+model), CI/CD, model registry , feature store , automation.
Governance: audit trails, explainability, human-in-the-loop, security .
Drive user adoption — unused models earn zero ROI.
Plan operations budget and eventual model retirement .
Learnings feed the next iteration → back to Phase I .
knowledgeCheck: Why is "deploy and forget" fatal for AI systems but merely risky for ordinary software?

bullets: "Deployment is a birthday, not a funeral" — the model's life starts at go-live.

examTips.heading: Traps
bullets: Any " deploy and the project is complete " option → wrong.
"Models don't need retraining" → wrong (drift!).
"Roll out to 100% immediately" in high-stakes cases → prefer staged rollout.
"Monitoring = server uptime" → incomplete; include performance/drift/KPI/fairness.

title: The 7 Patterns of AI
subtitle: Universal classification of AI use cases
examWeightHint: No pattern match ⇒ probably not an AI problem.
top10: Every AI use case maps to one or more of the 7 patterns — no match ⇒ not AI.
Hyperpersonalization = segment of one (recommendations, offers).
Autonomous = acts with minimal human involvement (not scripted RPA).
Predictive = forecast + decision support (human decides).
Conversation = NLP/chat/voice/sentiment/translation.
Patterns & Anomalies = fraud, intrusion, odd-one-out ← fraud lives HERE.
Recognition = identify things in unstructured media (OCR, vision, speech-to-text).
Goal-Driven = reinforcement learning, rewards, optimal strategy.
Patterns combine — scope iteration 1 around one pattern (start small).
Patterns are technology-independent problem shapes, mapped in Phase I .
revision: 7 Patterns = universal classification of AI use cases ; no pattern match → probably not AI.
1 Hyperpersonalization — segment of one; recommendations, tailored offers.
2 Autonomous Systems — acts with minimal human help; vehicles, robots, agents.
3 Predictive Analytics — forecast outcomes, decision support; churn, default, demand.
4 Conversation & Human Interaction — chatbots, voice, NLP, sentiment, translation.
5 Patterns & Anomalies — fraud, intrusion, odd-one-out, associations.
6 Recognition — identify things in images/audio/video/docs; OCR, face, tumor.
7 Goal-Driven Systems — reinforcement learning; optimize via rewards.
Patterns are technology-independent and combine in real systems.
Used in Phase I for AI validation; imply data/skill needs for later phases.
Fraud ≠ Recognition — it's Patterns & Anomalies (classic trap).

examTips.heading: Memory Tricks
bullets: Mnemonic sentence: " H appy A unts P repare C hai, P akode R oz G arma-garam" → H yperpersonalization, A utonomous, P redictive, C onversation, P atterns&Anomalies, R ecognition, G oal-driven. 🍵

examTips.heading: Keyword → Pattern Reflexes
